On 22 April 1500 a Portuguese fleet under Pedro Álvares Cabral sighted the coast of what is now Brazil and claimed it for Portugal. The fleet of 13 ships had left Lisbon bound for India, following the route opened by Vasco da Gama, and swung far west into the Atlantic to catch the winds.

The crews landed near today's Porto Seguro, met the local Tupi people, and held a mass. The scribe Pero Vaz de Caminha wrote a long letter to the king describing the land and its people, often called Brazil's birth certificate. Under the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 this land fell in Portugal's half of the world.

Cabral sent one ship home with the news and sailed on to Calicut. At first Portugal cared little for the new land beyond the red dye wood that gave Brazil its name and the brazilwood trade. Real settlement began in the 1530s and grew into Portuguese Brazil.
